prompt: Which sentence describes REST rather than something often mistaken for it?
hint: Fielding's idea fits in one sentence.

choices.text: Any API that sends JSON over HTTP, whatever its addresses look like
choices.why: Plenty of JSON-over-HTTP APIs are one address and a POST for everything, which is RPC.

choices.text: A protocol, published by the IETF as an RFC
choices.why: REST is an architectural style from a thesis, not a protocol.

choices.text: A library for building web servers
choices.why: No library is involved; shelf is REST with Python's standard library alone.

choices.text: Addressed resources, used through HTTP's own methods
choices.why: Right. Addresses name things; GET, PUT and DELETE say what to do.

prompt: Why can ten copies of a REST server run behind one load balancer without sharing memory?
hint: Think about what a request carries.

choices.text: Because each copy keeps the conversation in memory
choices.why: Then a client's next request, sent to another copy, would find nothing.

choices.text: Because the load balancer remembers each client's state
choices.why: A balancer forwards requests; it does not hold the application's state.

choices.text: Because each request carries what is needed to answer it
choices.why: Right. No memory of the conversation is needed, so any copy can answer.

choices.text: Because JSON is stateless
choices.why: JSON is a format; statelessness is a property of how the server is designed.

prompt: Match each style to what a request names.
hint: The table in the first section.

pairs.right: an operation described in a WSDL

prompt: Why does the course recommend a virtual machine over installing the packages on the computer you use?
hint: What matches the transcripts?

choices.text: It runs faster than an installed system, because it has its own memory
choices.why: A VM adds a little overhead; speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Only a virtual machine runs the Python 3 version the course needs
choices.why: Python runs on every system; the point is having the same versions.

choices.text: The same system and packages everywhere, and disposable
choices.why: Right. Same outputs as the lessons, and nothing left behind on your own system.

choices.text: The platform provides it
choices.why: The platform provides no machine; you build it.

prompt: Your transcripts show `ubuntu@api` where the lesson shows `ana@api`. What does that mean?
hint: Who is Multipass's user?

choices.text: Nothing to fix; Multipass names its user ubuntu
choices.why: Right. Only the prompt differs.

choices.text: The machine was built with the wrong release
choices.why: The release is in /etc/os-release, not in the user's name.

choices.text: Create a user called ana before going on
choices.why: Nothing in the course depends on the user's name.

choices.text: You are logged in as root
choices.why: Root's prompt ends in # and is called root.

prompt: The import check prints `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'grpc'`. What do you install?
hint: The table pairs each package with a lesson.

choices.text: `protobuf-compiler`
choices.why: That is the protoc command; the Python module grpc comes from another package.

choices.text: `python3-grpcio`
choices.why: Right. It provides the module named grpc.

choices.text: `python3-graphql-core`
choices.why: That one provides graphql, for lesson 3.

choices.text: `python3-pip`, then `pip install grpc`
choices.why: The course installs from Ubuntu's archive; only lesson 6 uses pip.

prompt: How many Python libraries does the import check in the section load?
hint: Count the names after `import`.

prompt: Where do the books live, so that stopping `rest.py` loses nothing?
hint: Look at what the first request created.

choices.text: In `shelf.db`
choices.why: Right. db.py creates it on first use; the program only reads and writes it.

choices.text: In `rest.py`'s memory
choices.why: Memory is lost when the process stops.

choices.text: In `__pycache__`
choices.why: That holds compiled Python, not data.

choices.text: In the second terminal
choices.why: The terminal only shows the server's log.

prompt: While `rest.py` was being written, a refused form body came back as a request called `title=Quincas`. What caused it?
hint: The note beside `parse_request`.

choices.text: curl sent the form twice, once as the body and once as a request of its own
choices.why: curl sent one request; the server misread what was left.

choices.text: The unread body stayed in the connection and became the next request
choices.why: Right. That is why the class now reads the whole request first.

choices.text: HTTP/1.1 does not allow a body in a POST, so the server read it as a new request
choices.why: POST bodies are normal; this one was simply never read.

choices.text: A 415 always closes the connection
choices.why: Nothing closed it, which is exactly the problem.

prompt: The first line of every file the course gives you is a comment naming its ___.
hint: So a copied file can say where it belongs.

prompt: `python3 rest.py` ends with `OSError: [Errno 98] Address already in use`. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Port 8000.

choices.text: db.py is missing from the directory rest.py runs in
choices.why: A missing module fails on import, with a different error.

choices.text: The machine has no network, so the server cannot open a port
choices.why: 127.0.0.1 needs no network at all.

choices.text: Port 8000 is below the range an ordinary user may open
choices.why: Only ports below 1024 do.

choices.text: An earlier rest.py still running in another terminal
choices.why: Right. `ss -ltnp 'sport = :8000'` names it.

prompt: What exit code did `curl` give when nothing was listening on port 8000?
hint: `echo $?` printed it.

prompt: Put the steps that set up the machine in the order the lesson gives them.
hint: From your computer's terminal to the API.
items: sudo apt-get install -y curl jq sqlite3 …
python3 rest.py, in a second terminal
trap: Update the package lists before installing.

prompt: Which address names one item rather than a collection?
hint: An item ends in an id.

choices.text: `/v1/books`
choices.why: That is the collection of every book.

choices.text: `/v1/authors/2/books`
choices.why: A collection inside an item: it ends in `books`.

choices.text: `/v1/books?author_id=3`
choices.why: The same collection, filtered.

choices.text: `/v1/books/3`
choices.why: Right. It ends in an id.

prompt: Why does shelf put a book's `id` in its address rather than its ISBN, which is also unique?
hint: Addresses get stored by other people.

choices.text: An identifier from the world gets corrected, breaking stored addresses
choices.why: Right. The system's own id never changes and is never reused.

choices.text: ISBNs are too long for a URL
choices.why: Thirteen digits fit easily.

choices.text: SQLite searches a text column like the ISBN far slower than an integer id
choices.why: It can; the column is indexed by UNIQUE.

choices.text: REST forbids text in addresses
choices.why: `/v1/books` is text.

prompt: A client wants Saramago's books and, tomorrow, books by year and by price. Which design serves that best?
hint: Is a book something that stands on its own?

choices.text: Filtering `/v1/books` with query strings
choices.why: Right. One collection, cut any number of ways.

choices.text: `/v1/authors/3/years/1995/prices/5990/books`
choices.why: Nesting every criterion makes paths nobody can build.

choices.text: A new endpoint per criterion, such as `/v1/getBooksByYear`
choices.why: A verb in the path, and one address per question.

choices.text: POST the criteria to `/v1/books`
choices.why: POST creates; reading is GET.

prompt: In REST the address names a thing, and the HTTP ___ says what to do with it.
hint: GET, PUT, DELETE.

prompt: Match each method to what it does to a resource.
hint: The table at the top of the section.

pairs.right: replaces it with the body, whole
changes only the fields the body names

prompt: The second identical `DELETE /v1/books/7` answered 404. Is DELETE still idempotent?
hint: Idempotence is about one thing.

choices.text: No, because the two answers differ
choices.why: Idempotence is about the server's state, not the answer.

choices.text: Only if the server answered 204 twice
choices.why: The same state is what counts, and it is the same.

choices.text: Yes: either way, book 7 is gone
choices.why: Right. A retrying client reads the 404 as already done.

choices.text: No, DELETE is never idempotent
choices.why: HTTP defines DELETE as idempotent.

prompt: A mobile app's connection drops before it hears the answer to a request. Which request can it send again without thinking?
hint: Which methods promise that a second copy cannot hurt?

choices.text: `POST /v1/books` with a new book
choices.why: A second POST may create a second book.

choices.text: `PATCH /v1/books/7` with `{"stock": 5}`, because every PATCH is idempotent
choices.why: This one is, but the method does not promise it, and the client cannot know.

choices.text: `PUT /v1/books/7` with the whole book
choices.why: Right. PUT promises idempotence: the book ends up the same.

choices.text: None of them; HTTP has no such guarantee
choices.why: It does, for GET, PUT and DELETE.

prompt: A new book answered 201 Created, and the ___ header said where it lives.
hint: Its value was /v1/books/7.

prompt: Why did shelf refuse `PUT /v1/books/7` with the body `{"stock": 5}`?
hint: What does PUT do with fields it was not sent?

choices.text: Stock is fixed when a book is created and cannot change afterwards
choices.why: PATCH changed it a moment later.

choices.text: Book 7 had been deleted by then, so there was nothing to replace
choices.why: It did; that would have been a 404.

choices.text: PUT replaces the whole book; this body is incomplete
choices.why: Right. 422, missing fields. PATCH is the method for one field.

choices.text: The body was not valid JSON, because the number had no quotes
choices.why: It was; that would have been a 400.

prompt: A body arrives labelled `application/json` and reads `{"title": `. Which code fits it?
hint: The label is right; the bytes are not.

choices.why: 415 is about the label, which is right here.
422 is for JSON that parses and breaks a rule.
Right. The bytes are not valid JSON.
The server did not fail; the request is wrong.

prompt: Your API answers 500 when a client sends malformed JSON. What does every well-behaved client do next?
hint: What does 5xx tell a client?

choices.text: Stops, since 5xx means the request is wrong
choices.why: That is what a 4xx would have told it.

choices.text: Asks the user to log in
choices.why: That is 401's meaning.

choices.text: Follows the Location header
choices.why: That is 3xx.

choices.text: Retries, later, a request that will never succeed
choices.why: Right. 5xx says the server failed, so retrying looks reasonable.

prompt: Match each request to shelf to the code it got.
hint: The captures in this section and the two before it.

prompt: Which of these codes tell a client that sending the same request again, unchanged, will fail again?
hint: The first digit is the class.

choices.why: Right. 4xx: the request is wrong.
5xx: the server failed; later may work.
Right. 4xx: fix the label first.
5xx: the request may be fine.

prompt: What did Python's library answer to `OPTIONS /v1/books`, and what should shelf have answered?
hint: The method exists in HTTP.

choices.text: 501 as HTML; 405 as JSON with `Allow`
choices.why: Right. 501 is for a method the server does not recognise at all.

choices.text: 404 as HTML; 404 as JSON
choices.why: The address exists; only the method is refused.

choices.text: 405 as JSON; nothing else, it was right
choices.why: It was 501, with an HTML page.

choices.text: 500 as JSON; 200 with an empty body
choices.why: It was 501, and 200 would claim it worked.

prompt: Which status code means "I know who you are, and no"?
hint: 401 is the other one.

prompt: Which change to shelf's version 1 needs a new version?
hint: Could an existing client break?

choices.text: Adding a `pages` field to every book
choices.why: A client that does not read it never notices.

choices.text: Adding a `/v1/publishers` collection
choices.why: Nobody was calling it, so nobody breaks.

choices.text: Accepting an optional `?year=` filter
choices.why: Old requests work exactly as before.

choices.text: Turning `price_cents` into an object
choices.why: Right. Every client that read the number breaks.

prompt: Why does the course prefer the version in the path?
hint: Think of a log line at night.

choices.text: It is the most faithful to HTTP
choices.why: That is the media type's argument, not the path's.

choices.text: It shows in every log line, link and bug report
choices.why: Right. Seeing the version when something breaks is what matters most.

choices.text: Browsers refuse custom headers
choices.why: They send them; it is caches that must be told.

choices.text: It keeps each resource at one single address for all its versions
choices.why: It does the opposite: two addresses for one resource.

prompt: The two headers that announce a version is on its way out are `Deprecation` and ___.
hint: It carries the date it stops answering.

prompt: A partner asks for `GET /v1/deleteBook?id=4`. What is wrong with it, by the lesson's rules?
hint: Two rules at once.

choices.text: Only that ids go in the query string
choices.why: Ids go in the path; but the GET is the dangerous part.

choices.text: A verb in the address, and a GET that changes something
choices.why: Right. It should be DELETE /v1/books/4; a crawler following links would empty the shop.

choices.text: Nothing at all, as long as the partner documents what it does
choices.why: Documentation does not change what proxies and crawlers assume about GET.

choices.text: It lacks a version
choices.why: It has /v1.

prompt: Order what shelf checks when a PATCH arrives, from first to last.
hint: Read `rest.py` from `parse_request` to `write`.
items: the whole request is read, body included
the address names one version-1 book
the body is labelled JSON and parses into an object
the fields are known and have the right types
the database's CHECK and foreign key accept it
trap: The address is checked before the body.

prompt: Which of these are breaking changes for a client of `/v1/books/{id}`?
hint: Removed, renamed or retyped.

choices.text: renaming `stock` to `in_stock`
choices.why: Right. Clients reading stock get nothing.

choices.text: sending `year` as a string
choices.why: Right. A type change breaks arithmetic and comparisons.

choices.text: adding a `language` field
choices.why: Additive: invisible to clients that ignore it.

choices.text: removing `isbn`
choices.why: Right. Anything reading it breaks.
